content.title: comments on #1487
content.review:
This paper proposes a new contrastive method that adaptively mines hard positive pairs during the training process. Two variants of it include pretraining based version (AdpCLR^pre) and fully trained version (AdpCLR^full), which also gives theoretical analysis on convergence rate and generalization and is consistent with experiment results. AdpCLR^pre outperforms state-of-the-art contrastive-based models by 3.0% with extra 100 epochs while AdpCLR^full is over by 2.5% with additional 600 epochs. 

pros:
1. The main contribution of this paper is to propose an adaptive way to find out positive pairs sampled from two different categories with data augmentation, which expands the distribution of positive pairs. It can increase the generalization ability of the framework. 
2. The proposed approach AdpCLR is the balance of supervised contrastive method and SimCLR, so it should be slightly more accurate than SimCLR and less accurate than supervised contrastive method. The experiment results demonstrate this.
3. Since it’s novel to my best knowledge of mining positive pairs. I think it’s interesting to explore these positives and it’s a valuable addition to the field.

cons:
1.	Experiment configurations: 
On Overall comparison with state-of-the-art of Section 4.2, it could be more clear to present the number of training epochs and the choice of K(the number of top-K nearest neighbors for one image) for AdpCLR$^{pre}$. And it's better to point out the best K and batch size pair in the paper.
2.	Hyper-parameter transferability:
This paper shows that the choice of K is closely related with the batch size and has great effect on the final performance. One of my concerns is that for different datasets and backbones, are the optimal K values and batch sizes given in the paper still the best?
3.	Theoretical analysis on hard positive pairs: 
Although Table 4 presents F1-score with different K and batch size, showing that the error rate of pseudo labels decreases gradually, it remains to see if the dot product of two feature vectors is the best way to measure the similarity of two images. The distribution of feature vectors corresponds to that of dataset. It is interesting to see which way to measure the similarity of two images with which portion of feature vectors could have better performance.
4.	Some typos:
(1)	On the title of Table 4, the value of batch size is missing.
(2)	On the third last line of the second last paragraph of page 7, it should be ‘After 1000 epochs of boosting training’.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: 1`487 Review
content.review:
This paper proposes a new contrastive method, which fills the gap between self-supervised contrastive learning and supervised contrastive learning. Pseudo-labeling point view is used to construct positive and negative labels for sample pairs.

Strengths：
1. This paper learn the self-supervised model from the perspective of positive and negative pair samples, which may be an interesting and useful point. The idea of mining positive pairs is interesting, especially in self-supervised domain.
2. Existing self-supervised contrastive-based method mainly focus on negative pairs mining. It is interesting to explore hard positive pairs in this domain. The experiment results also demonstrate the power of positives.
3. This paper provides a theoretical guarantee for the upper bound generalization error and the convergence rate of the proposed model; And the experimental results on ImageNet are consistent with their theoretical analysis.

Weaknesses and suggestions to this paper.
1. The setting of symbols and the expression of formulas are sometimes not clear and rigorous enough in Sec 3.2. For example, what is the difference between $z_i^1$, $z_i^2$ and $z_i$; the similarity matrix $S$ is also not well defined. And does typos exist in Eq.3? 
2. The x-axis coordinates in Fig.2 looks disproportionate. Is this setting intentional? It's better to explain why for this setting.
3. While pre-trained AdpCLR can outperform the accuracy of SimCLR 3.0%, I'd still like to see if the fully-trained AdpCLR perform under different backbones (resnet-50(1x, 2x)). It is better to add some results of AdapCLR$^{full}$ in Table 1.
4. Authors theoretically analyzed the effect of different K and batch size. By set K=1 and K=5, which both outperform the accuracy of SimCLR. But why did only try K=1 and K=5, but not more K values?
5. Table 3 shown in plot might be better than in table.

content.title: Reproducibility and writing is concern
content.review:
The paper proposes a self-supervised learning model where, in each batch set of positive pair are used to increase the positive support set. These positive pairs are selected as top-K most similar pair after encoding the samples. The paper also provides the generalization error and convergence rate. The paper shows the improved result on the ImageNet dataset on the ResNet-50 (1x,2x,4x) architecture. Also, compared to the base model simCLR the proposed model shows the slow convergence rate.

Positive:
1: Instead of using a single positive pair, K positive pair provides richer information; therefore, the performance gain is expected. At the same time, we have to ensure that the positive pair are true positive pair; otherwise, performance may drop quickly. 

2: Paper shows the consistently improved result on the ImageNet dataset for the ResNet-50 (1x,2x,4x) architecture compared to the baseline simCLR.

3: Ablation over the different setup like K value, batch size and epoch are properly provided.

Possible weakness:
1: AdpCLR_pre looks intuitive since it uses a pre-trained self-supervised model (simCLR); therefore, we can get a high-quality similarity measure in the pair of image embedding. While in the AdpCLR_full author mentioned that no pre-trained model is used then only we can ensure that P_same is the correct pair and rest of the top-K pair we can not guarantee anything.  Because the similarity measure on any other embedding vector will not be of high quality and incorrect pair will degrade the result more compared to the correct one. How will you get the correct top-K positive pair in the AdpCLR_full setup? Maybe I am missing something, or the proper explanation is not provided. In the Algorithm, if pretrain=False the encoder F will be random and it will provide poor embedding, hence we expect poor similarity measure.
Please explain the process of embedding in the case of AdpCLR_full if no pre-trained is used.

2: I believe the convergence and generalization should be a function of the number of incorrect positive pair. In the generalization error, we can see that it is a function of K, but at the same time, the error will depend on the expected error in the positive pair. It is counter-intuitive AdpCLR_full convergence does not have any dependency on the correct positive pair or the positive pair. If we have few/may incorrect positive pair the learning will be too difficult, and convergence will slow down, or it will oscillate and will not converge at all. Please provide a detail explanation.

3: The experimental settings are not mentioned properly; result reproducibility is critical using the provided information. The author does not provide the code. 


4: can you provide the result for the AdpCLR_full approach for the ResNet-50 (1x,2x,4x) architecture like the result provided for AdpCLR_pre in the table-1.

5: How the pseudo label is defined?

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2.
content.comment:
Thanks for your questions.

\textbf{Q1} AdpCLR\_pre looks intuitive since....\\
\textbf{A1:} As you said, $AdpCLR^{pre}$ is more intuitive (and more convincing) than $AdpCLR^{full}$, because before the second stage training, encoder has been well trained to extract features, thus the top-$K$ will be more reliable as expanded positives. In terms of $AdpCLR^{full}$ or similarly SimCLR which also is trained from scratch, when the batch size is set large, more true positive pairs can be mis-labeled as negative pairs. So the question also relates to why SimCLR can converge when batch size is 8192 (even for batch size is 32768, see Figure B.2 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.05709.pdf)? Intuitively, although some negative pairs are mis-recognized as positives, we have the $\mathcal{P}_{same}$ and a large number of rest negative pairs to provide to make it converge. The experimental result is consistent with SimCLR: when given larger batch size, the error rate of pseudo label is increasing, then, the convergence rate will decrease (see Figure B.2).

\textbf{Q2} I believe the convergence and generalization should be....\\
\textbf{A2:} We provide two training strategies. For $AdpCLR^{pre}$, we suppose the pre-trained encoder can correctly identify a certain ratio of false negative samples (i.e. expanded positives) out of the current batch, i.e. $\lambda l$ samples, where $\lambda \in [0,1]$ is the ratio and $l$ is the batch size. So the final convergence of $AdpCLR^{pre}$ is related to $\lambda$ i.e correctly identified positive pair. For $AdpCLR^{full}$, due to $l >> K$, or simply we suppose none of correct positive pair is recognized as positive pairs at the initial stage. So it is only related to $K$. We will further clarify it in our final version.

\textbf{Q3:} The experimental settings are not mentioned....\\
\textbf{A3:} We can provide the $\mathcal{L}_{adp}$ at this moment. The pre-trained model will be available after reviewing stage. 
\begin{lstlisting}
def forward(self, z_i, z_j):
    batch_size = z_i.size(0)
    out = torch.cat([z_i, z_j], dim=0)      # [2*B, 2*B]
    sim_matrix = torch.exp(torch.mm(out, out.t().contiguous()) / self.temperature)
    mask = (torch.ones_like(sim_matrix) - torch.eye(2 * batch_size, device=sim_matrix.device)).bool() # [2*B, 2*B-1]
    sim_matrix = sim_matrix.masked_select(mask).view(2 * batch_size, -1)
    top_sim = torch.topk(sim_matrix, dim=-1, k=self.k)[0]
    same_sim = torch.exp(torch.sum(z_i * z_j, dim=-1) / self.temperature) # [2*B]
    same_sim = torch.cat([same_sim, same_sim], dim=0)
    pos_sim = torch.cat([same_sim.unsqueeze(1), top_sim], dim=-1)
    loss = (- torch.log(pos_sim.sum(dim=-1) / sim_matrix.sum(dim=-1))).mean()
    return loss
\end{lstlisting}

\textbf{Q4} Can you provide the result for the $AdpCLR_{full}$....\\ 
\textbf{A4:} Because it is indeed time consuming for experimenting with $AdpCLR^{full}$, so far we haven't conducted experiments on Resnet-50 (2x, 4x). While we will try to add some relevant experiments in our next version.

\textbf{Q5} How the pseudo label is defined?\\
\textbf{A5:} If two images belong to one category, we regard the label as 1, otherwise 0.

content.title: Simple idea and works well.
content.review:
This paper develops AdpCLR: Adaptive Contrastive Learning Representations, which is an extension of contrastive-based self-supervised learning. They are the first to involve the hard-positive pairs mining, while the previous works mainly focus on negative mining.

Pros:
1. Positive pairs and negative pairs are usually not specifically defined in contrastive learning domain, but due to the success of supervised contrastive learning, which proves that the definition of positives in SimCLR (images augmented from the same images are positives) is not the best. This paper re-define positives (images belongs to top-$K$ closest embedding set), and their method AdpCLR can mine these hard positives automatically. The provided f1 scores show that their approach can really mine these pairs.
2. This paper gives the upper bound and convergence rate of generalization error. The experimental results are in line with the theoretically analyze.
3. This paper mainly conduct experiments on ImageNet. The experimental results show they outperform all the existing contrastive-based self-supervised learning. 


Cons:
1. The paper is not well written, there are some typos and some information is clearly delivered. I suggest the authors shall carefully proof-read the paper in the new version.
2. I wonder why only K=1 and K=5 are given for their experimental results, how the performance on other settings of K?
3. Under the definition of positives in this paper, I wonder can this idea be applied in other self-supervised learning methods, such as MOCO, BYOL, to get better results?

content.title: Failed to reproduce
content.comment:
Hi authors,

I tried to re-implement your method hard, but still can not get it work.  My training pipeline is:

(1) train standard SimCLR using Lars for 1000 epochs, get 69.4% accuracy.

(2) Retrain the encoder using $L_{adp}$. For this stage, I strictly follow your paper: train for extra 100 epochs; initial learning rate is 0.15 x bsz / 256; weight decay is 1e-6; also use Lars. 

But one unclear part in equation (5) of this paper is that, it uses $L_{in}^{sup}$ in "Supervised Contrastive Learning" paper (See eq (2),(3), and Table 1 in the SupCon paper https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.11362.pdf). So I played with both $L_{in}^{sup}$ and $L_{out}^{sup}$ to check.

Here is the results after 1100 epochs (1000 epoch SimCLR + 100 epochs AdaCLR fine-tuning):

loss                      k =  0        1         2          3          4 

$L_{out}^{sup}$                         68.5    68.6   65.4    64.4    62.7

$L_{in}^{sup}$                         68.6    68.5   63.2    60.4    0.3

If I perform $AdpCLR^{full}$, i.e., no pre-training and directly train with $L_{adp}$ for 1000 epochs. For this case, I used a fix top-k of 5. Then I get:

$L_{out}^{sup}$    0.5%

$L_{in}^{sup}$     0.2%

It basically just crashes. I wonder if there is some important caveat that I am missing? 

Extra question, for Table 4, how is the F1 score computed? My understanding is that, for bsz=4096, each image will have on average 3 other images from the same class. Then you will have (6+1) positives, because each image will have 2 views, plus you get another view of the same image. Then when you set K=5, in my mind the best recall you can get is $5/7=0.714$, but you reported 0.875. I wonder which part I am misinterpreting? 

Thank you!


==== updated ====

Also a related work is missing.

Tian et al. Contrastive multiview coding. ECCV 2020.

content.title: Response to Yonglong Tian
content.comment:
Thanks for your interest to our work as well as spending the time for checking and reproducing our methods. 

There are some points may be helpful for your notice:

1) In the first stage of $AdpCLR^{pre}$ i.e. directly running the source code of SimCLR for training our own model, we recall that we only got $67.x\%$ accuracy (sorry for forgetting the exact number). So in the experiments of our paper, we directly use the pre-trained model provided in https://github.com/tonylins/simclr-converter and https://github.com/google-research/simclr to catch up the performance. 

2) You mentioned for $K=0$ (that means it degenerates to SimCLR), additional 100 epochs after 1000 epochs will lead the accuracy decrease to 68.5\%. But Fig. B.2 in the SimCLR paper shows that the corresponding accuracy tends to be above 69\% for batchsize=4096, and they mentioned that the performance seems to saturate with a batch size of 8192, while training longer can still significantly improve the performance. Our experiments show the consistent conclusion in Table 2. 

3) The similarity metric is important, since with different metrics, the top-$K$ may change. Please try to use \textbf{normalized} dot product (which is our choice in our experiments) or cosine similarity. We will clarify it in our next version.

4) We carefully read your code and paper, both $L_{out}^{sup}$ and $L_{in}^{sup}$ are not the same with our $\mathcal{L}_{adp}$. As we know, $\mathcal{L}_{info}$ can be divided into two parts i.e alignment and uniformity. As the positive pairs are not fully correct, if the objective lose some uniformity part, it may obtain degenerate  solution. So we suggest you follow the Eq.~5 in our paper.

\textbf{About F1}.  

1) For $BatchSize=4096$, there will be roughly 3*2+1 positive pairs (computed by: $K=3$ and two versions of augmented samples leads to 3*2 expanded positives, plus the augmented version of the vanilla positive sample) and the rest 8184 negative pairs in each row (in total 8191). This setting is exactly following the protocol in SimCLR that one time of data augmentation is performed on the input positive samples, and twice are performed on the rest samples in each batch that are regarded as negative ones in SimCLR, and the learning is performed using the augmented version of samples but NOT using the original samples.

For your interest on our case when $K=5$, here we give more detailed explanation in case you miss some information in our paper. In line $12^{th}$ in Algorithm 1, we said before taking the top-$K$ closest samples to positive pairs, we technically mask the similarity value of the original input positive themselves -- this follows the protocol in the code of SimCLR to exclude the raw positive samples in the loss -- recall the example in the above paragraph we discuss.

Besides, the positive set is the union of $\mathcal{P}_{same}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{adp}$. So in your case, the mean of best F1 should be 0.923 and the worst F1 is 0.154. For F1 computation, you can refer to https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.f1\_score.html.

2) Back to the first problem, in combination of F1, we suggest you strictly follow the algorithm in our paper.

\textbf{About AdpCLR$^{full}$. } After reading your comments, we carefully checked our code again. We find there indeed exist a  problem on evaluation of AdpCLR$^{full}$. On training stage, we adopted $\mathcal{L}_{adp}$ to train, while in evaluation stage, we only used require\_grad=False, which causes the parameters of encoder function not strictly frozen. As a result, the reported results of AdpCLR$^{full}$ are overestimated. But there's no problem for AdpCLR$^{pre}$, so for re-production of AdpCLR$^{pre}$, we suggest you strictly follow the algorithm in our paper.

In conclusion, thanks for your questions. We will re-work the AdpCLR$^{full}$, and we may provide experiment results in our next version. Thanks!

content.title: Further comment
content.comment:
Hi Authors,

Thanks for your response. Now the portal is reopened, and I can share my thoughts on your response now:

1. "In the first stage of  i.e. directly running the source code of SimCLR for training our own model, we recall that we only got  67.x accuracy (sorry for forgetting the exact number). So in the experiments of our paper, we directly use the pre-trained model provided in..."


    Just wonder if you failed to reproduce the original SimCLR performance, how do you get the numbers in Table 2-4? Are they based on and improved upon your baseline of 67.X?


2. "You mentioned for K=0 (that means it degenerates to SimCLR), additional 100 epochs after 1000 epochs will lead the accuracy decrease to 68.5%....while training longer can still significantly improve the performance..."


    The reason why we further fine-tuned a 69.4% SimCLR model for another 100 epochs with your objective but only get 68.5%, is that the learning rate get reset as your paper mentioned. In the first 1000 epochs, base lr decreases from 0.3 sample to 0 with a cosine schedule, but later when fine-tune for 100 epochs, the base lr jumps up to 0.15 suddenly, and it changes the optimization dynamics. That's why it's different from directly training 1100 epochs with smooth learning rate. I am not sure whether you observed similar stuff or not.


3. "The similarity metric is important, since with different metrics, the top- may change. Please try to use \textbf{normalized} dot product (which is our choice in our experiments) or cosine similarity."


    In my experiments mentioned initially, I strictly followed cosine similarity.

4. "We carefully read your code and paper, both $L^{sup}_{in}$ and ... are not the same with our L{adp} ..."


    In fact, $L^{sup}_{in}$ is equivalent to your objective, the only difference is a constant co-efficient. If you compare them carefully, you will see that in both $L^{sup}_{in}$ and your $L_{adapt}$, inside the \log, the numerator sums all positive logits, while the denominator sums all logits (positive logits + negative logits). 

5. "we said before taking the top-K closest samples to positive pairs, we technically mask the similarity value of the original input positive themselves -- this follows the protocol in the code of SimCLR to exclude the raw positive samples in the loss..."


    Thanks for trying to explain, but yeah I know it. I think maybe you missed what I was talking about, so let me explain again in details. In each batch of 4096 images belonging to 1000 classes, roughly each image will get 3 other images that belong to the same class, then for each crop of a given image, it will have 7 positives (already exclude itself), by 3 * 2 + 1. So, you will have 7 positives actually, right? Then when K=5, suppose all the 5 closest points are positives, then the recall is 5/7, and the precision is 1.0, right? then do F1 = 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall) = 0.8333. This is the upper bound, so you could not get 0.875, right? But it's OK since you seems to have removed this table in your update.


6. "Back to the first problem, in combination of F1, we suggest you strictly follow the algorithm in our paper"


    I think I at least followed what was written in the paper, especially Algorithm 1.


p.s., just curious, what hard-ware was used to run all these experiments in table 2-4. Seems you have run ~100 1000-epoch SimCLR, which is quite computationally prohibitive if we are not Google. Also, if you could release the code for other people to verify and reproduce the results, that would be super helpful.

Thanks,
Yonglong
